docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Known limitations and issues, with their root causes and resolutions.

docs.title: Library not found
docs.text:
Symptom. litertlm.New (or litertlm.Load) returns "litert-lm" not found; checked: ... listing several paths.

Cause. The LiteRT-LM shared library is not at any of the locations the loader searches.

Search order (when WithLib is empty):

  1. LITERTLM_LIB environment variable.
  2. Platform default paths:
    • Linux/macOS/FreeBSD: $XDG_DATA_HOME/litertlm/lib, ~/.litertlm/lib, /opt/litertlm/lib, /opt/homebrew/lib (macOS only), /usr/local/lib.
    • Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\litertlm\lib, %PROGRAMFILES%\litertlm\lib.

The default library short-name is litert-lm (liblitert-lm.so, liblitert-lm.dylib, litert-lm.dll), falling back to legacy backend-specific names (litertlm_c_cpu / litertlm_c) when absent. Override it with WithLibName("...") or LITERTLM_LIB_NAME.

Fix. Either:

  • Pass WithLib("/abs/path/to/lib") to litertlm.New.
  • Set LITERTLM_LIB=/abs/path/to/lib.
  • Symlink your lib directory into one of the default paths above.

docs.title: Garbage or repetitive output from low-level Session APIs
docs.text:
Symptom. Low-level Session.GenerateContent or Session.RunPrefill / Session.RunDecode returns one of:

  • An empty string, or resp.Text(0) == "".
  • A single token repeated until max output tokens is reached (0000000000…, …, <bos><bos>…).
  • A short hallucinated phrase repeated (**{sea}** **{sea}** **{sea}**).
  • A coherent first sentence that then loops (Marco who set out one morning to catch fish. Marco who set out one morning to catch fish. …).

Cause. Chat-tuned models (Gemma instruct, Qwen, Llama-Instruct, …) are fine-tuned with a chat template wrapping every conversation turn (for example, Gemma's <|turn>user …<turn|> <|turn>model ). Raw Session.GenerateContent and Session.RunPrefill / Session.RunDecode forward your prompt bytes as-is unless SessionConfig.SetApplyPromptTemplate(true) and a model template handle are active. Without template framing, chat-tuned models frequently emit an immediate end-of-turn token or degenerate into repetition loops.

Fix. Use the high-level Client.Generate, Client.GenerateStream, or Chat APIs. Both Client.Generate* and Chat.Send* open a Conversation under the hood, applying the model's chat template automatically:

chat, _ := client.NewChat(ctx, litertlm.WithSystemPrompt("You are a friendly assistant."))
defer chat.Close()

reply, _ := chat.Send(ctx, "Explain why the sky is blue.")
fmt.Println(reply.Text())

To curb repetition loops during open-ended generation, apply per-turn logit penalties with WithRepetitionPenalty and WithNoRepeatNgram (see examples/logit-penalties/).

When driving raw Session prefill/decode directly without a template, supply completion-style prefixes the base distribution can extend ("The capital of France is") or branch from checkpoints built with SaveCheckpoint / RewindToCheckpoint.

docs.title: Detokenized output contains ▁ (U+2581) instead of spaces
docs.text:
Symptom. Engine.Detokenize returns text with the lower-one-eighth- block character ▁ where you'd expect ASCII spaces:

"Hello,▁world.▁How▁are▁you?"

Cause. That's SentencePiece's internal space marker. The C API faithfully passes through the tokenizer's raw output without post-processing it.

Fix. Fix in Go if you want plain spaces:

docs.title: Empty default.profraw files appear in working directory
docs.text:
Symptom. Running anything that loads the LiteRT-LM library leaves a zero-byte default.profraw file in the current working directory.

Cause. The prebuilt LiteRT-LM dependencies under prebuilt/<os>/lib*.so were compiled with LLVM -fprofile-instr-generate. The embedded __llvm_profile_* runtime writes a coverage dump on process exit to ./default.profraw.

Fix. Set LLVM_PROFILE_FILE to a discardable target before running:

Linux/macOSWindows 
LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=/dev/null \
LITERTLM_LIB=/path/to/lib \
    go run main.go

$Env:LLVM_PROFILE_FILE = "NUL"
$Env:LITERTLM_LIB = "$Env:USERPROFILE\litertlm\lib"
go run main.go

docs.title: engine_create fails with DYNAMIC_UPDATE_SLICE errors
docs.text:
Symptom. litertlm.New (or low-level NewEngine) errors during construction; the C-side log mentions DYNAMIC_UPDATE_SLICE.

Cause. WithMaxTokens(n) is set below the model's smallest prefill signature (typically 128).

Fix. Use WithMaxTokens(1024) or higher. The high-level Client defaults to 4096, which works for every Gemma 4 variant.

docs.title: ErrUnimplemented: missing C symbol or API minor-version mismatch
docs.text:
Symptom. A call into the Go API returns an error wrapping litertlm.ErrUnimplemented (*litertlm.CError with Code: StatusUnimplemented):

litertlm: missing C symbol "litert_lm_session_config_set_apply_prompt_template"
in loaded library (refresh prebuilt LiteRT-LM libs)

Or for features gated behind a newer C API minor version:

litertlm: version_check: requires LiteRT-LM C API 1.1+, loaded library is 1.0.0 (Unimplemented)

litertlm.Load validates the major C API version (1.x) and returns early; per-symbol lookup happens lazily on first use of a method, so version-specific symbols fail with ErrUnimplemented when invoked against a build that does not export them.

Cause. The LiteRT-LM library staged in $LITERTLM_LIB does not export the requested symbol or reports an earlier C API minor version. Features requiring 1.1+ include WithSelectedSignatures / EngineSettings.SetSelectedSignatures, WithToolChoice / OptionalArgs.SetToolChoice, PlanModelSync / SyncModel / SyncModelCache, and WithDebuggerEnabled / EngineSettings.SetEnableDebugger. Speculative decoding Lenience != 0 also requires a runtime exporting litert_lm_speculative_decoding_config_set_lenience.

Fix. Match error handling with errors.Is(err, litertlm.ErrUnimplemented), leave optional fields at their defaults (Lenience: 0), or stage a newer LiteRT-LM shared library release (minimum supported base is v0.19.1 per LITERTLM-BUILD.md).

docs.title: Failed to create GemmaModelConstraintProvider
docs.text:
Symptom. Opening a chat with WithConstrainedDecoding(true) (or WithConstraintProvider(...)) fails during NewChat:

litertlm: NewChat: litertlm: conversation_create: INTERNAL: Failed to create GemmaModelConstraintProvider. (Internal)

Cause. Grammar-constrained decoding requires constraint-provider metadata embedded inside the .litertlm model file. Compact models without embedded constraint-provider metadata (for example, gemma3-270m-it-q8.litertlm) cannot initialize a constraint provider.

Fix. Use a model containing constraint metadata (such as gemma3-1b-it-int4, gemma-4-E2B-it, or Qwen3-0.6B) for grammar constraints, or use GenerateData[T] without WithConstrainedDecoding(true).

docs.title: UNIMPLEMENTED: Sampler type: 3 not implemented yet
docs.text:
Symptom. Creating a session or conversation with SamplerGreedy (SamplerType = 3, returned by DefaultSamplerParams()) fails on CPU with StatusUnimplemented.

Cause. Greedy sampler type 3 is not implemented on the CPU executor in LiteRT-LM v0.19.1.

Fix. Use SamplerTopP with Temperature: 0 for deterministic sampling (litertlm.SamplerParams{Type: litertlm.SamplerTopP, TopK: 40, TopP: 0.95, Temperature: 0, Seed: 1}), or omit SetSamplerParams / WithDefaultSampler to use the model's built-in sampler configuration.

docs.title: GPU run falls back to CPU
docs.text:
Symptom. Running with WithBackend("gpu") logs WARNING: GPU accelerator could not be loaded and registered and inference continues on CPU.

Cause. On Windows, DirectX Shader Compiler binaries (dxcompiler.dll, dxil.dll) are missing from $LITERTLM_LIB, or an older split build is missing GPU accelerator plugins (libLiteRtWebGpuAccelerator.*, libLiteRtTopKWebGpuSampler.*). Unified liblitert-lm builds bundle the LiteRT GPU accelerator internally.

Fix. Stage dxcompiler.dll and dxil.dll on Windows (automatic with libfetch.Fetch(..., libfetch.WithBackend("gpu"))), or re-stage the shared library files per LITERTLM-BUILD-WINDOWS.md and LITERTLM-BUILD.md.

docs.title: tool_calls.arguments numeric values come as float64
docs.text:
Symptom. reply.ToolCalls()[0].Function.Arguments["count"].(int) panics with "interface conversion: interface {} is float64, not int".

Cause. encoding/json decodes JSON numbers into float64 by default. The Go Arguments map is map[string]any, and the model emits all numbers as JSON numbers regardless of the schema you declared.

Fix. Type-assert to float64 and convert if needed:

n := int(reply.ToolCalls()[0].Function.Arguments["count"].(float64))

docs.title: conversation_send_message failed on Qwen3 multi-turn
docs.text:
Symptom. Chat.Send (or low-level Conversation.SendMessage) returns an error wrapping *CError on conversation_send_message on the second turn of a Qwen3 conversation, and RenderMessage on the same turn fails in conversation_render_message_to_string.

Cause. Qwen3's Jinja chat template calls reasoning_content.strip('\n') when rendering the prior assistant turn's <think>...</think> block. LiteRT-LM's embedded Jinja implementation does not provide a string.strip(chars) method, so the template aborts before any decode runs. Reproducible against the upstream litert_lm_advanced_main.exe --multi_turns=true binary, so the bug is wholly in upstream LiteRT-LM.

Fix. None available in litertlm-go. Single-turn flows (Client.Generate, Client.GenerateStream, GenerateData[T]) work on Qwen3. Track upstream LiteRT-LM for a Jinja strip(chars) implementation or a patched Qwen3 chat template.

Smaller Qwen3 variants (e.g. 0.6B) may render turn 2 without hitting the failing template branch but can still emit <|endoftext|> and Human: continuation patterns past their stop tokens on long outputs.

docs.title: Markers <|"|> in tool-call argument values
docs.text:
Symptom. A tool-call argument has the literal text <|"|>Boston, MA<|"|> instead of Boston, MA.

Cause. Gemma 4's chat-template renderer leaves its internal quote markers in string-typed arguments when the C side surfaces them as JSON.

Fix. The high-level *Reply strips these automatically on parse, so callers see clean values. If you're working at the low level (Conversation.SendMessage), you will need to strip them yourself:

strings.ReplaceAll(arg, `<|"|>`, "")

docs.title: GPU process crashes on Windows (Exception 0xc0000005)
docs.text:
Symptom. Running GPU-backed inference crashes the test or application process with a memory access violation (0xc0000005).

Cause. Graphics API drivers and shader compilers (e.g., Direct3D 12/WebGPU loaded via libwebgpu_dawn.dll) cannot compile shaders or manage TLS state on the background worker threads managed by Go's runtime scheduler.

Fix. Execute client initialization and inference calls on the operating system's primary main thread. Avoid executing them inside concurrent goroutines or tests without thread locking (runtime.LockOSThread()).

docs.title: Failed to create engine (INTERNAL: ERROR: [unknown:0])
docs.text:
Symptom. Client initialization fails early during engine creation with: Failed to create engine: INTERNAL: ERROR: [unknown:0]

Cause. Custom source builds splitting the C API from auxiliary GPU plugin libraries linked libLiteRt statically instead of dynamically, preventing delegate registration.

Fix. Prefer building upstream's unified target (//c:litert-lm) from LITERTLM-BUILD.md. For split source builds with separate plugin libraries, compile with --define=litert_runtime_link_mode=dynamic and ensure $LITERTLM_LIB contains libLiteRt and libwebgpu_dawn on PATH / LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

docs.title: Your First Local LLM App in 5 Minutes
docs.text:
Running an open-weights model directly inside a Go process removes the operational overhead of managing external inference servers or separate container runtimes. In this tutorial, you build a complete Go command-line program that fetches the LiteRT-LM shared library, downloads a compact Gemma 3 model, inspects its capabilities before loading weights, streams tokens live to standard output, and reports per-turn throughput benchmarks.

~5 min Text & Streaming gemma3-1b-it-int4 CPU or GPU

docs.title: Step 1 — Create Your Go Module
docs.text:
Start from an empty project directory, initialize a Go module, and add litertlm-go as a dependency:

mkdir local-llm-demo
cd local-llm-demo
go mod init local-llm-demo
go get github.com/vladimirvivien/litertlm-go@latest

docs.title: Step 2 — Fetch Runtime Binaries & Model Weights Automatically
docs.text:
Instead of asking users to download zip archives and export environment paths beforehand, your program can call litertlm.FetchLib and litertlm.FetchModel. Both helpers verify checksums and store artifacts in your user cache directory so subsequent runs start immediately offline.

Attach litertlm.WithModelProgress to render clean download progress while weights stream from Hugging Face:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "runtime"
    "time"

    "github.com/vladimirvivien/litertlm-go/pkg/litertlm"
)

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()

    // 1. Download and cache official LiteRT-LM shared libraries for this host.
    libDir, err := litertlm.FetchLib(ctx, runtime.GOOS, runtime.GOARCH, "v0.19.1")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("FetchLib failed: %v", err)
    }

    // 2. Download and cache Gemma 3 1B (quantized int4) from Hugging Face.
    modelPath, err := litertlm.FetchModel(ctx, "litert-community/gemma3-1b-it-int4",
        litertlm.WithModelProgress(func(downloaded, total int64, pct float64) {
            if total > 0 {
                fmt.Printf("\rDownloading model: %.1f%% (%.1f / %.1f MB)",
                    pct, float64(downloaded)/1e6, float64(total)/1e6)
            }
        }),
    )
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("FetchModel failed: %v", err)
    }
    fmt.Println()

docs.title: Step 3 — Inspect Model Capabilities Before Booting
docs.text:
Large .litertlm files embed capability metadata—context limits, supported modalities (text, vision, audio), thinking support, tool-calling compatibility, and default sampling settings. Calling litertlm.Load followed by litertlm.InspectModel reads that header without allocating tensor weights or KV caches, making it ideal for startup validation:

    if err := litertlm.Load(libDir, "cpu", ""); err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Load failed: %v", err)
    }
    maj, minVer, pat, err := litertlm.APIVersion()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("APIVersion failed: %v", err)
    }
    caps, err := litertlm.InspectModel(modelPath)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("InspectModel failed: %v", err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("LiteRT-LM C API %d.%d.%d | type=%s max_ctx=%d vision=%v thinking=%v tools=%v\n",
        maj, minVer, pat, caps.ModelType, caps.MaxContextTokens,
        caps.SupportsVision(), caps.SupportsThinking, caps.SupportsFunctionCalling)

docs.title: Step 4 — Stream Tokens & Measure Throughput
docs.text:
Initialize a Client with litertlm.WithBenchmarkEnabled() so the runtime records time-to-first-token (TTFT) and prefill/decode speeds. Always defer client.Close() to release native engine handles cleanly when the function returns.

Pair context.WithTimeout with client.GenerateStream (which returns a Go iter.Seq2[litertlm.Chunk, error] iterator) to print each token as soon as the model decodes it, then run client.GenerateResponse when you want structured benchmark numbers alongside the reply:

    litertlm.SetMinLogLevel(litertlm.LogQuiet)

    client, err := litertlm.New(ctx,
        litertlm.WithLib(libDir),
        litertlm.WithModel(modelPath),
        litertlm.WithBackend("cpu"),
        litertlm.WithMaxTokens(2048),
        litertlm.WithBenchmarkEnabled(),
    )
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("New client failed: %v", err)
    }
    defer client.Close()

    runCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 60*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    fmt.Println("--- Streaming Reply ---")
    for chunk, err := range client.GenerateStream(runCtx, "Explain why Go uses goroutines in three sentences.") {
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatalf("GenerateStream failed: %v", err)
        }
        fmt.Print(chunk.Text)
        if chunk.Final {
            fmt.Println()
        }
    }

    fmt.Println("--- Timed Response & Benchmark ---")
    resp, err := client.GenerateResponse(runCtx, "Give one tip for writing clean concurrent Go code.")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("GenerateResponse failed: %v", err)
    }
    fmt.Println(resp.Text())

    if b := resp.Benchmark(); b != nil {
        fmt.Printf("TTFT: %v | KV Cap: %d tokens\n", b.TimeToFirstToken, b.MaxNumTokens)
        for i, tps := range b.DecodeTokensPerSec {
            fmt.Printf("Decode turn %d: %.1f tok/s (%d tokens)\n",
                i, tps, b.DecodeTokenCounts[i])
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Run & Expected Output
docs.text:
Run your program with a single command:

go run .

(Host-specific timings and throughput numbers differ.)

LiteRT-LM C API 1.0.0 | type=LLM max_ctx=32768 vision=false thinking=false tools=true
--- Streaming Reply ---
Go uses lightweight goroutines instead of heavy operating-system threads so programs can launch thousands of concurrent tasks with minimal memory overhead. The Go runtime multiplexes goroutines onto a small pool of OS threads automatically. Paired with channels, this makes concurrent workflows simple to write and reason about.

Pass a `context.Context` into blocking or streaming calls so cancellation propagates cleanly when work is no longer needed.

docs.title: Local Multimodal Semantic Search & Zero-Shot Classification
docs.text:
Dedicated embedding models convert text paragraphs, images, and audio recordings into dense numerical vectors inside a single shared coordinate space. Once artifacts live in that space, you can search across modalities by meaning rather than exact keywords—matching a text query like "aerial view of parked cars" directly to overhead photography—and classify unseen files zero-shot with no task-specific training data. In this tutorial, you vectorize inputs with litertlm.EmbeddingClient, build a persistent cross-modal index using the search and classify packages under examples/semantic-search, and shrink vector storage using Matryoshka truncation.

~10 min Embeddings & Retrieval EmbeddingGemma 2 (Ungated) Text · Image · Audio

docs.title: Choosing a Multimodal Embedding Model
docs.text:
LiteRT-LM models built for vector retrieval report ModelTypeEmbedding from InspectModel. Public, ungated EmbeddingGemma 2 weights on Hugging Face download directly via litertlm.FetchModel without access tokens:

Model Identifier Modalities Download Size Native Vector Dim litert-community/embeddinggemma-2-text-270m-litert-lm Text ~165 MB 768 litert-community/embeddinggemma-2-text-vision-440m-litert-lm Text + Vision ~388 MB 768 litert-community/embeddinggemma-2-740m-litert-lm Text + Vision + Audio ~485 MB 768

Check any .litertlm artifact with examples/capabilities before indexing:

go run ./examples/capabilities -get-lib v0.19.1 -get-model litert-community/embeddinggemma-2-text-vision-440m-litert-lm

docs.title: Step 1 — Compute Vectors Directly with EmbeddingClient
docs.text:
Unlike generative LLMs (litertlm.New), standalone embedding models open via litertlm.NewEmbeddingClient. Pass WithNormalize(true) so cosine similarity simplifies to a fast dot product, and WithOverflowStrategy(litertlm.OverflowChunkAndAverage) so long documents exceeding the encoder sequence window are automatically chunked and averaged instead of failing:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "runtime"

    "github.com/vladimirvivien/litertlm-go/examples/semantic-search/classify"
    "github.com/vladimirvivien/litertlm-go/examples/semantic-search/search"
    "github.com/vladimirvivien/litertlm-go/pkg/litertlm"
)

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()

    libDir, err := litertlm.FetchLib(ctx, runtime.GOOS, runtime.GOARCH, "v0.19.1")
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }

    modelPath, err := litertlm.FetchModel(ctx, "litert-community/embeddinggemma-2-text-vision-440m-litert-lm")
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }

    if err := litertlm.Load(libDir, "cpu", ""); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    caps, err := litertlm.InspectModel(modelPath)
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    if caps.ModelType != litertlm.ModelTypeEmbedding {
        log.Fatalf("expected embedding model, got %s", caps.ModelType)
    }

    litertlm.SetMinLogLevel(litertlm.LogQuiet)
    embedder, err := litertlm.NewEmbeddingClient(ctx,
        litertlm.WithLib(libDir),
        litertlm.WithModel(modelPath),
        litertlm.WithBackend("cpu"),
    )
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    defer embedder.Close()

    // Single normalized embedding vector:
    vec, err := embedder.Embed(ctx, "Go concurrency with goroutines",
        litertlm.WithNormalize(true),
        litertlm.WithOverflowStrategy(litertlm.OverflowChunkAndAverage),
    )
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    fmt.Printf("Embedded vector length: %d (vision supported=%v)\n", len(vec), caps.SupportsVision())

docs.title: Step 2 — Index Mixed Files & Query Across Modalities (search)
docs.text:
Rather than writing boilerplate directory walkers and cosine-ranking loops by hand, import examples/semantic-search/search. Its Index applies EmbeddingGemma's asymmetric retrieval prefixes (DefaultQueryPrefix / DefaultDocumentPrefix), batch-embeds text documents, calls EmbedMulti on image or audio files, saves JSON snapshots cleanly, and scores queries by cosine similarity:

    cfg := search.DefaultConfig()
    cfg.EnableVision = caps.SupportsVision()
    cfg.EnableAudio = caps.SupportsAudio()

    idx := search.New(embedder, cfg)
    stats, err := idx.IndexDir(ctx, "./examples/testdata")
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    fmt.Printf("Indexed %d items (%d text, %d image) in %v\n",
        stats.Indexed, stats.TextCount, stats.ImageCount, stats.Duration)

    // Query both text descriptions and raw images with a natural-language phrase:
    matches, err := idx.QueryText(ctx, "overhead aerial photograph of a parking lot with rows of cars", 4)
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    for i, m := range matches {
        fmt.Printf("%d. %.4f [%-5s] %s\n", i+1, m.Score, m.Entry.Modality, m.Entry.ID)
    }

    // Persist to disk for instant offline reloads:
    if err := idx.Save("index.json"); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }

docs.title: Step 4 — Shrink Indexes with Matryoshka Truncation
docs.text:
EmbeddingGemma 2 models are trained with Matryoshka representation learning, meaning the leading coordinates carry the strongest semantic signal. Passing litertlm.WithOutputSize(256) (or -dim 256 on the CLI, supporting 128, 256, or 512) cuts index size and scoring cost by 3x while retaining strong retrieval accuracy:

smallVec, err := embedder.Embed(ctx, "parked sedans from above",
    litertlm.WithNormalize(true),
    litertlm.WithOutputSize(256),
)

On search.Config and classify.Config, set OutputDim: 256 so both indexed documents and incoming queries truncate to matching 256-dimensional vectors.

docs.title: Tool-Calling Agents & KV-Cache Branching
docs.text:
Turning a local model into a reliable assistant takes two primitives: letting the model invoke typed Go functions safely, and branching conversations cheaply without paying prompt prefill costs twice. In this tutorial, you build a multi-hop tool-calling agent with RegisterTool, add error-recovery policies, concurrency caps, and ToolChoice constraints, and fork prefilled conversation state using Chat.Clone and low-level KV checkpoints.

~12 min Tools & KV Cache gemma3-1b-it-int4 / Gemma 4 High & Low Level

docs.title: Step 1 — Register Typed Go Tools with Auto-Dispatch
docs.text:
litertlm.RegisterTool uses Go reflection over your input struct to generate an OpenAI-style JSON Schema automatically. Field names come from json tags (or lowercased field names), non-pointer fields become required parameters, and description struct tags guide the model on what values to pass.

Attach registered tools to a Chat using WithTool(...). When chat.Send runs, litertlm-go intercepts any tool calls emitted by the model, invokes your Go handler, feeds the serialized result back into the conversation, and returns the final natural-language answer—all inside a single chat.Send call:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "runtime"

    "github.com/vladimirvivien/litertlm-go/pkg/litertlm"
)

type WeatherIn struct {
    City string `json:"city" description:"City name to check weather for, e.g. Tokyo"`
}

type WeatherOut struct {
    City       string  `json:"city"`
    TempC      float64 `json:"temp_c"`
    Conditions string  `json:"conditions"`
}

var weatherDB = map[string]WeatherOut{
    "Tokyo":  {City: "Tokyo", TempC: 22, Conditions: "clear"},
    "Boston": {City: "Boston", TempC: 15, Conditions: "breezy"},
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    libDir, err := litertlm.FetchLib(ctx, runtime.GOOS, runtime.GOARCH, "v0.19.1")
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    modelPath, err := litertlm.FetchModel(ctx, "litert-community/gemma3-1b-it-int4")
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }

    litertlm.SetMinLogLevel(litertlm.LogQuiet)
    client, err := litertlm.New(ctx, litertlm.WithLib(libDir), litertlm.WithModel(modelPath))
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    defer client.Close()

    lookupWeather, err := litertlm.RegisterTool(client, "lookup_weather",
        "Return current weather conditions for a city.",
        func(_ context.Context, in WeatherIn) (WeatherOut, error) {
            out, ok := weatherDB[in.City]
            if !ok {
                return WeatherOut{}, fmt.Errorf("no forecast found for %q", in.City)
            }
            return out, nil
        },
        // Inform-on-error lets the model recover if an unknown city is queried:
        litertlm.WithToolPolicy(litertlm.ToolPolicyInformOnError),
    )
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }

    chat, err := client.NewChat(ctx,
        litertlm.WithSystemPrompt("You answer weather questions using lookup_weather. If a lookup fails, apologize or try a nearby city mentioned by the user."),
        litertlm.WithTool(lookupWeather),
        litertlm.WithMaxToolHops(4),
    )
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    defer chat.Close()

    reply, err := chat.Send(ctx, "Check Atlantis weather; if unavailable, check Tokyo.")
    if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
    fmt.Println(reply.Text())
}

docs.title: Bounded Tool Loops & Error Recovery
docs.text:
• WithMaxToolHops(n) caps model-to-tool round-trips (default 5) so an indecisive model cannot loop indefinitely. When exceeded, check errors.Is(err, litertlm.ErrToolHopsExceeded) or unwrap *litertlm.ToolHopsError for partial replies.
  • ToolPolicyReturnOnError (the default) immediately aborts chat.Send and returns the Go error. Choose it for authorization failures or corrupted state.
  • ToolPolicyInformOnError serializes {"error": "..."} back into the conversation so the model can apologize, adjust arguments, or fall back to another tool call.

docs.title: Step 2 — Run Concurrent Tool Batches & Enforce ToolChoice
docs.text:
When a model requests several independent tool calls in a single turn (for example, looking up two cities simultaneously), pass litertlm.WithMaxConcurrentTools(4) on chat.Send. Handlers execute concurrently in worker goroutines up to the specified limit, while results are stitched back into the conversation in the exact call order the model produced. Make sure concurrent handlers synchronize access to shared mutable state.

On LiteRT-LM C API 1.1.0+, you can also compel or restrict tool usage per turn via WithToolChoice when opening a chat with WithConstrainedDecoding(true):

forcedChat, err := client.NewChat(ctx,
    litertlm.WithConstrainedDecoding(true),
    litertlm.WithTool(lookupWeather),
)
if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
defer forcedChat.Close()

reply, err := forcedChat.Send(ctx, "How is Boston today?",
    litertlm.WithMaxOutputTokens(64),
    litertlm.WithToolChoice(litertlm.ToolChoiceFunction("lookup_weather")),
)
if errors.Is(err, litertlm.ErrUnimplemented) {
    log.Println("WithToolChoice requires a LiteRT-LM C API 1.1+ shared library")
}

Available policies include ToolChoiceAuto(), ToolChoiceNone(), ToolChoiceRequired(), ToolChoiceFunction(name), ToolChoiceAllowedTools(mode, names...), and ToolChoiceRawJSON(payload).

docs.title: Step 3 — Branch Prefilled Conversations with Chat.Clone
docs.text:
Prefilling long system prompts, style rules, or reference documents can take hundreds of milliseconds on edge CPUs. Rather than rebuilding a Chat from scratch for each parallel candidate or speculative follow-up, call chat.Clone() after prefilling shared context. Each clone starts with an independent KV cache pointing at identical history and must be closed cleanly while keeping the root Chat open:

chat, err := client.NewChat(ctx,
    litertlm.WithSystemPrompt("You are a concise assistant. Answer in one short sentence."),
)
if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
defer chat.Close()

if _, err := chat.Send(ctx, "Remember: Comet is a tricolor corgi who loves fetching tennis balls."); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

branchB, err := chat.Clone()
if err != nil {
    if errors.Is(err, litertlm.ErrUnimplemented) {
        log.Println("Loaded executor does not support Session.Clone yet")
        return
    }
    log.Fatal(err)
}
defer branchB.Close()

replyA, _ := chat.Send(ctx, "What breed is Comet?")
replyB, _ := branchB.Send(ctx, "Suggest a playful nickname for Comet.")
fmt.Println("Branch A:", replyA.Text())
fmt.Println("Branch B:", replyB.Text())

docs.title: Step 4 — Checkpoint & Rewind at the Low-Level Session Layer
docs.text:
When you need explicit byte-level prompt control (such as tree-of-thought search or reusable completion prefixes without chat-template wrapping), drop down to engine.NewSession with SaveCheckpoint, RewindToCheckpoint, Session.Clone, and RunDecodeAsyncCh:

session, err := client.Engine().NewSession(0)
if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
defer session.Delete()

prefix, _ := litertlm.NewTextInputString("In a small seaside village,")
defer prefix.Delete()

_ = session.RunPrefill([]litertlm.InputData{prefix})
_ = session.SaveCheckpoint("after-prefix")

clonedSess, err := session.Clone()
if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
defer clonedSess.Delete()

// Decode Branch A on session, rewind KV cache, then decode Branch B cleanly:
inA, _ := litertlm.NewTextInputString(" an old lighthouse keeper")
defer inA.Delete()
_ = session.RunPrefill([]litertlm.InputData{inA})
for sc := range session.RunDecodeAsyncCh() {
    if sc.Err != nil { log.Fatal(sc.Err) }
    fmt.Print(sc.Text)
}
fmt.Println()

_ = session.RewindToCheckpoint("after-prefix")

docs.title: Vision Q&A & Structured JSON Extraction
docs.text:
Local multimodal models can read receipts, inspect UI screenshots, analyze photographs, and return clean Go structs without uploading images to a third-party API. In this tutorial, you configure a vision-enabled Client, ask natural-language questions about an image, extract typed Go structs with GenerateDataMulti[T], and contrast that approach with decode-time grammar constraints (WithConstraint).

~10 min Vision + Structured Data Gemma 4 E2B / E4B CPU or GPU

On-device image understanding and structured JSON extraction running locally via litertlm-go.

docs.title: Step 1 — Configure a Vision-Capable Client
docs.text:
Multimodal .litertlm artifacts pair a text decoder with a separate vision encoder. Two client options matter specifically when handling images:

  1. litertlm.WithVisionBackend("cpu") (or "gpu"): Enables the vision executor. Leaving it unset disables image inputs even when the model file includes a vision encoder.
  2. litertlm.WithMaxTokens(4096) (or higher): Image patches expand into hundreds of visual tokens during prefill; a small token budget (such as 512) leaves too little headroom for both visual tokens and output text.
package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "runtime"

    "github.com/vladimirvivien/litertlm-go/pkg/litertlm"
)

func openVisionClient(ctx context.Context, modelIDOrPath string) (*litertlm.Client, error) {
    libDir, err := litertlm.FetchLib(ctx, runtime.GOOS, runtime.GOARCH, "v0.19.1")
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    modelPath, err := litertlm.FetchModel(ctx, modelIDOrPath)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    litertlm.SetMinLogLevel(litertlm.LogQuiet)
    return litertlm.New(ctx,
        litertlm.WithLib(libDir),
        litertlm.WithModel(modelPath),
        litertlm.WithBackend("cpu"),
        litertlm.WithVisionBackend("cpu"),
        litertlm.WithMaxTokens(4096),
    )
}

Verify Vision Support First

Before booting an engine, check caps, err := litertlm.InspectModel(modelPath) and confirm caps.SupportsVision() is true.

docs.title: Step 2 — Run Free-Form Vision Q&A (GenerateMulti)
docs.text:
Pass an ordered slice of litertlm.Part values into client.GenerateMulti. Helper constructors such as litertlm.ImageFromFile detect the image MIME type from file extensions (jpeg, png, webp, gif, bmp) and validate the bytes before calling native code:

func describeImage(ctx context.Context, client *litertlm.Client, imagePath string) error {
    img, err := litertlm.ImageFromFile(imagePath)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    reply, err := client.GenerateMulti(ctx, []litertlm.Part{
        img,
        litertlm.Text("Describe the objects visible in this image in two crisp sentences."),
    })
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    fmt.Println("=== Vision Description ===")
    fmt.Println(reply)
    return nil
}

client.GenerateMulti runs as a single independent turn. If you want to follow up with additional questions referencing the same uploaded image without re-encoding image patches, open a Chat and call chat.SendMulti followed by chat.Send.

docs.title: Step 3 — Extract Typed Go Structs (GenerateDataMulti[T])
docs.text:
Unstructured descriptions are great for human readers, but backend pipelines need predictable fields. litertlm.GenerateDataMulti[T] inspects any Go struct T, synthesizes a JSON capture tool (or schema hint fallback), retries on malformed responses via litertlm.WithRetries, and returns a populated *T:

type Scene struct {
    Description string   `json:"description"`
    Objects     []string `json:"objects"`
}

func extractScene(ctx context.Context, client *litertlm.Client, imagePath string) error {
    img, err := litertlm.ImageFromFile(imagePath)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    scene, err := litertlm.GenerateDataMulti[Scene](ctx, client,
        []litertlm.Part{
            img,
            litertlm.Text("Extract a one-sentence scene description and list every distinct object."),
        },
        litertlm.WithRetries(2),
    )
    if err != nil {
        var gd *litertlm.GenerateDataError
        if errors.As(err, &gd) {
            return fmt.Errorf("extraction failed during %s after %d attempt(s): %w",
                gd.Phase, gd.Attempts, gd.Err)
        }
        return err
    }

    encoded, _ := json.MarshalIndent(scene, "", "  ")
    fmt.Println("=== Extracted Struct ===")
    fmt.Println(string(encoded))
    return nil
}

docs.title: Step 4 — Lock Syntax at Decode Time (WithConstraint)
docs.text:
When your target .litertlm model embeds constraint-provider metadata (including Gemma 3 1B, Gemma 4 E2B, and Qwen 3 0.6B), Chat can enforce decode-time token masking via LLGuidance. Instead of validating JSON after generation finishes, invalid syntax tokens are masked out before sampling—guaranteeing structurally valid JSON or exact regex matches on every turn:

const personSchema = `{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "name": { "type": "string" },
    "age":  { "type": "integer" }
  },
  "required": ["name", "age"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}`

func runConstrainedTurns(ctx context.Context, client *litertlm.Client) error {
    chat, err := client.NewChat(ctx,
        litertlm.WithConstrainedDecoding(true),
        litertlm.WithConstraintProvider(litertlm.ConstraintProviderLLGuidance),
    )
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer chat.Close()

    r1, err := chat.Send(ctx,
        "Extract the person's name and age from: Ada Lovelace was 36 years old.",
        litertlm.WithMaxOutputTokens(64),
        litertlm.WithConstraint(litertlm.ConstraintJSONSchema, personSchema),
    )
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Println("JSON Schema output:", r1.Text())

    r2, err := chat.Send(ctx,
        "Is Paris in France? Answer yes or no.",
        litertlm.WithMaxOutputTokens(16),
        litertlm.WithConstraint(litertlm.ConstraintRegex, `(yes|no)`),
    )
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Println("Regex output:", r2.Text())
    return nil
}

docs.title: Choosing Between GenerateData[T] and WithConstraint
docs.text: Capability GenerateData[T] / GenerateDataMulti[T] WithConstraint (LLGuidance) Works on every .litertlm model Yes (falls back to prompt schema + tolerant parser) Requires embedded constraint metadata in model Output target Populated Go struct *T Raw JSON string or regex-matched text Multi-turn chat compatible One-shot helper Per-turn inside Chat or Client.Generate* Supports regex grammars JSON objects & schemas Arbitrary JSON Schema and regular expressions

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Step-by-step walkthroughs help you move from a blank go.mod file to running real local AI workflows inside your own Go binaries. Each tutorial focuses on one end-to-end capability—streaming inference, vision-to-JSON extraction, multimodal semantic search, and branching tool-calling agents—so you can learn each pattern with copy-ready Go code and runnable repository examples.

Before You Begin

Every tutorial needs only Go 1.26 or newer. Native LiteRT-LM shared libraries (v0.19.1+) and public .litertlm models are fetched and cached automatically on first run via litertlm.FetchLib and litertlm.FetchModel.
